The different elements of the story work together seamlessly to create a unified and satisfying character portrait. The opening and middle sections establish Ilse's deep-rooted connection to the river, her physical competence, and her comfort within the harsh, predictable routines of operating the cable ferry. Every detail—from her knowledge of the regular passengers to her confidence in the ferry cable despite the blinding fog—builds up her quiet resilience and belonging in this world. This careful setup gives emotional weight to the ending, when the phone call from her son (presumably) introduces the central conflict: the pressure for her to retire, sell the ferry rights, and leave her home. Her decision to zip the vibrating phone back into her pocket and focus both hands on docking the ferry is a logical and satisfying conclusion that ties her established character directly to the central theme of holding onto one's way of life.
